newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers seek to ease embargo against Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers seek to ease embargo against Cuba.

text.p: A bipartisan group of lawmakers on Wednesday introduced legislation to lift the decades-old embargo on food and medicine to Cuba, saying it was time for limited trade with the Communist-ruled island.

The proposal, sponsored by four Republicans and eight Democrats in the House of Representatives, was immediately attacked by Cuban-American lawmakers as playing into the hands of President Fidel Castro's government.

The bill did not yet have a sponsor in the Senate, where ultra-conservative Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina was expected to oppose any measure to ease the 35-year-old U.S. sanctions against the Caribbean island of 11 million people.
The White House said it was concerned about conditions in Cuba and would examine the proposed legislation carefully given that the embargo makes provisions for humanitarian aid.

The House members said their proposal would help children, the sick and the elderly in Cuba. Since the collapse of its trading partner, the former Soviet Union, Cuba has been forced to ration milk, rice, beans, chicken and other food staples.
Although the island offers world-class medical care for international patients able to pay in hard currency, ordinary Cubans are often unable to obtain an aspirin or other basic medicines.

The bill's sponsors were flanked at a news conference by more than two dozen physicians, church leaders, attorneys and academics who support a change in U.S. policy toward Cuba and an end to "the inhumane embargo of food and medicines."

Charles Rangel, the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, acknowledged that it would face a tough battle in the Senate, but the New York legislator was confident the bill would get to the floor of the House for debate this year.
Jim Leach, an Iowa Republican who heads the House Banking Committee, described U.S. policy toward Cuba as "one of the thorniest issues" in politics but said it was time to adopt more humane measures.
But lawmakers sympathetic to the mostly right-wing Cuban exile community in the United States immediately criticised the legislation as helping the Castro government.

"This bill is founded on a myth," said Representative Lincoln Diaz-Balart, who was accompanied in opposing the bill by fellow Florida Republican Ileana Ros-Lehtinen and Robert Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat.

"Cuba can buy medicines anywhere in the world. Nothing in the U.S. sanctions policy prohibits that," he said, adding that the U.S. government licensed more than $150 million in humanitarian assistance to Cuba over the past four years.

U.S. law permits sales of medicine and related equipment to Cuba, provided American companies meet licensing requirements, perform on-site inspections and follow procedures of the U.S. embargo. Critics of the embargo say the regulations are difficult to follow and intended to discourage U.S. companies from selling medical products to Cuba.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the Clinton Administration would study the legislation closely.

"We have been very concerned about the humanitarian conditions that face the people of Cuba. Those conditions arise becase of the nature of a very brutal, totalitarian regime," he told reporters when asked about the bill.

"Our policy is premised on the Cuban Democracy Act. There have been aspects of that legislation that allow for opening and liberalisation, in fact there are some specific provisions that allow for us to attend to those humanitarian conditions in Cuba," he said. "We work within the framework of that act, but this legislation of course we will examine carefully."
The embargo was toughened last year by the Helms-Burton Act, which seeks to stop foreign investment in Cuba and restricts ships from docking in the United States after stopping at Cuban ports.
Under this law, signed by Clinton after Cuba shot down two planes flown by Miami-based exiles, Washington has punished a Canadian mining firm and a Mexican industrial group.
